# Class Rules

## AI

When you do the exercises in this textbook you **should NOT** use AI.

Every line of code should be written by you, from your brain ✅🧠🙂 **NOT** from a robot brain ❌🤖.

If you use AI while you are learning to code for the first time, you will not learn how to code. You will not be able to debug and fix code when it goes wrong. 

Have a look at this [article](https://pxr687.github.io/doc_viewer/AI_assistance.pdf) which explains some of the bad effects of using AI when you are learning new coding skills. It says that:

- using AI when you learn will make you faster to finish coding tasks...

- ...*BUT* you will not understand the code you write, and you will be slower to learn the new skills.

Thinking is *hard*. It takes *effort*. But, like exercising and eating healthily, it is good for you.

Because thinking is hard, it feels good to let an AI think for you. Letting AI think for you, instead of thinking yourself, is called *cognitive offloading* - here are two quotes from the article linked above:

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pxr687/Intro_Comp_Programming/refs/heads/main/images/cognitive_offload.JPG)

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pxr687/Intro_Comp_Programming/refs/heads/main/images/cog_offload_2.JPG)

See the image below for a summary:

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pxr687/Intro_Comp_Programming/refs/heads/main/images/offloading.png)

So, cognitive offloading with an AI *feels* good, but it stops you learning. AI can be useful, for example, I used it to make the image above. BUT using Ai will stop you from learning to code, and it will make it harder for you to understand and debug code (either written by you, someone else, or an AI...).

So, for this course:

- 🧠✅

- 🤖❌

Do **NOT** try to secretly use AI in the class (me and the TA will be watching). In the exams and tests you will not have access to an AI. So, if you do use AI in the class you will break the class rules, and you will do badly in the exams and tests.

## Computers can make us stupid (even without AI)

```{note}
This section is adapted from [Brett, Rush, Adhikari, Denero and Wagner (2023)](https://odsti.github.io/cfd-textbook/surviving_computers.html). See the [license](https://github.com/pxr687/Intro_Comp_Programming/blob/main/license.md) page for more information.
```

Computers let us do lots of things we could not do without them. But they can also distract us
and make us dumb.

The computer has lots of nice colours, we can have 100s of browser tabs open,
we can have Youtube playing as we write code and video call our friends. You get the idea.

Our computer can take up enough mental energy that we stop thinking carefully about the task
we are doing. This is particularly dangerous when programming, because programming
needs careful logical thought.

For example, Muller et al (2014) found that when students listened to a lecture, those who took notes on paper
remembered more than those who took notes on a laptop.

As programmers, the students with the laptops are *us*. We have to be careful about the dumbing effect that using the computer can have, on our ability to think straight.

Experienced programmers know this problem, and they use tricks to deal with them.

Among these tricks, are the following.

## Have a piece of paper and a pen next to you

When _working_ on the computer, have a piece of paper and a pen next to you on your desk. 

When you notice that you don't fully understand an error or a task on the computer, stop, move the laptop out of the way, and write down your problem on a piece of paper. 

Give yourself some time to think about what the problem is, and how to solve it. 

Only then, you can return to the computer and try your solutions, or do more research. You will find that disengaging from the computer is a) difficult and b) very productive in releasing you from the various mental traps that it is easy to fall into when you get stuck on the computer.

Be like this guy, do not use AI, DO use a pen and paper:

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pxr687/Intro_Comp_Programming/refs/heads/main/images/be_like_him.png)

## Working together in class

When we are in class, you can talk to each other as your code. But you should write every line of code yourself (do not copy from others).

Again, you must use must your own brain, not your friend's brain, to write your code. As long as you do **NOT** copy any code, you can help each and support each other if you get stuck (there is a tip for how to do this in the next section). 

What is OK:

- Asking a friend for advice on how to fix a bug

- Pair programming (see the next section)

What is **not OK**:

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pxr687/Intro_Comp_Programming/refs/heads/main/images/copying.JPG)

> (Image made [here](https://imageresizer.com/meme-generator/edit/Mr-bean-copying)).

### Pair programming

One way of working together that you can use when completing the exercises in this textbook is *pair programming*. *Note*: this is *working together* where you are both thinking about and writing code as a team, it is not one person copying someone else's code, which is not allowed.

[Pair programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pair_programming) is
a technique that programmers use to improve the quality of their work
and accelerate learning. It is particularly useful early in learning, and with new tasks(Lui & Chan, 2006).

Pair programming has a standard form.

One member of the team is the _driver_. They sit in front of the keyboard and
type.

The other member of the team is the _navigator_. They do not use their own laptop, but watching the driver as they work, offering advice, and talking about ideas with the driver.

The pair should switch roles, for example, changing places for each exercise.

You will likely find that, when you are the driver, you think a lot slower
than the navigator, because you are thinking about two things, the task, and
interacting with the computer. When you switch to being the navigator, you
will find that you can think more quickly and carefully.
<!-- #endregion -->

## References

Kim Man Lui and Keith CC Chan. Pair programming productivity: novice–novice vs. expert–expert. International Journal of Human-computer studies, 64(9):915–925, 2006. URL: http://www.cs.utexas.edu/users/mckinley/305j/pair-hcs-2006.pdf.

Pam A Mueller and Daniel M Oppenheimer. The pen is mightier than the keyboard: advantages of longhand over laptop note taking. Psychological science, 25(6):1159–1168, 2014.
